title: The Latest Miami Design Trend Signals a Departure from Debauchery
summary:
While mega-clubs continue to rage, Miami’s once hedonistic hotel scene is shapeshifting into something more subdued.

The post The Latest Miami Design Trend Signals a Departure from Debauchery appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
At its heyday in the 1990s, the Rose Bar, the lobby lair at Delano Miami Beach, exemplified the city’s once-ravenous predilection for the debauched and the flashy. 

The illuminated quartz bar was always packed with Cosmo-sipping women in Manolos and the Hollywood set, including supermodels, actors, and A-List musicians like Lenny Kravitz, who designed the hotel’s nightclub, the Florida Room. Madonna was part-owner of the hotel’s Blue Door restaurant and celebrated her 37th birthday on the property.

In 1995, when visionary hotelier Ian Schrager and French designer Philippe Starck transformed the tired Art Deco beauty into an upscale destination resort, they simultaneously ignited a new chapter of anything-goes, wee-hours revelry.

“There were the cool rock star people, there were the Hollywood billionaire types, the downtown fashion New York people, people swimming naked in the pool at 1 am,” trainer David Barton, whose gym had a branch in the hotel for several years, told the New York Times. “You were just in this other world.”

That world may be dead—or, at least changing. 

After a multi-year, multimillion-dollar revamp, Delano Miami Beach has just reopened its doors with a classier, calmer vibe that’s more focused on wellness and fine dining than indulgence. Rose Bar may be back, but its surrealistic design with pink walls and lighting has given way to a cozier deep red, moody palette that is more about intimacy and connection than showing off.

There’s also a spa starring a 22-seat sauna and a private members’ retreat that signal a departure from clubby vibes and celebrity gawking to a less debaucherous form of socializing that resonates with today’s well-heeled travelers.

It’s not just the Delano that’s delicately balancing nostalgia with a fresh, contemporary aura. Art Deco and Miami Modern legends around town are in the midst of a rebrand.

A New Era of Miami Nightlife

Despite the mega-clubs that continue to rage, Miami’s hedonistic days are shapeshifting into something more subdued. As some of the city’s landmark hotels find new life, rowdiness is in the rearview mirror.

The 1940s Collins Avenue fixture, The Raleigh Hotel, which was spruced up by infamous hotelier André Balazs in 2004, is currently being developed by Rosewood Hotels & Resorts. Next year, the Auberge Collection is slated to unveil its reboot of the 1949, Albert Anis-designed Shore Club.

This latest turning point for the city and its tourism scene is proving that Miami’s Art Deco institutions are increasingly moving away from one-dimensional glamour and embracing the easygoing desires of contemporary travelers.

“What we are seeing globally, and Miami reflects this acutely, is a fundamental shift in what sophisticated travelers value. The era of purely scene-driven hospitality has given way to experiences that build intentionally, where dining, music, design, and atmosphere function as a single cohesive narrative rather than separate offerings,” explains Rizwan Kassim, CEO of Paris Society, the French hospitality company behind Rose Bar’s revitalization and the other food and beverage outlets in the Delano Miami Beach. 

For Gigi Rigolatto, a bright, boisterous restaurant buoyed by access to the Delano’s pool, Paris-based architect and designer Hugo Toro melded carved wood, yellow Siena marble, and coral stone. At the property’s Mimi Kakushi, the Dubai import that only guests and members can access, diners are transported to 1920s Osaka with wooden screens, hand-painted walls, and cinematic lighting courtesy of London studio Pirajean Lees. Conjuring these two disparate worlds was deliberate, Kassim points out, because “Miami has evolved significantly, and the hospitality landscape has had to evolve with it.”

In other Art Deco hotels, that evolution means honoring the natural scenery and culture. When overhauling the soon-to-open Royal Palm South Beach Miami, part of Marriott’s Tribute Portfolio collection, Malcolm Berg, president and design director of Coral Gables-based architecture and design firm EoA Group, opted for a restrained coastal sensibility mixing stone, wood, and plaster with stripes and sun-washed tones as opposed to the too-trendy, dated interiors defining the hotel’s most recent chapter. 

The new Royal Palm is “less about spectacle as identity and more about experience as daily life,” he says. To create what he calls “a continuous social landscape,” each individual space flows into one another including the fluid ensemble of F&B spaces that celebrate Miami’s motley neighborhoods. Cuban coffee and pastries call to mind Little Havana at Compass Rose, which uses the hotel’s vintage green-glass reception desk repurposed as a counter that evokes the Art Deco period. The poolside bar Paloma Club’s vivid yellow and blues speak to artsy neighborhoods like Wynwood. And the lush ambiance at rum bar, Mixed Company, encapsulates the exuberance of South Beach itself.

“The idea is that guests are almost on their own culinary tour through Miami as they move through the hotel, but it never feels forced,” says Garron Gore, senior director of restaurant & bar development at Davidson Restaurant Group. “There are still those fun, over-the-top moments Miami is known for, whether that is a tableside cocktail experience with glassware chilled to negative 40 degrees or fresh ceviche prepared tableside at the pool, but the overall atmosphere is more relaxed and approachable.”

Weaving in the ‘Tropical Deco’ Past

While these hotel redesigns are adapting to today’s laid-back travelers, they’re not necessarily shedding the Art Deco and Miami Modern accents that date back to the 1930s and ‘40s. The period, often dubbed “Tropical Deco,” provided a sleek, uplifting counterpoint to the long, gloomy Great Depression that had finally just faded away. The design teams responsible for the makeovers of these properties are carefully contemplating which elements to preserve.

For the Shelborne by Proper, the newest incarnation of the circa-1941 Collins Avenue property, Barcelona design studio ADC & Tuneu studied the original colors and lines of the Miami Modern property, such as the original ribbon windows and open-air breezeways, and the floating staircase that was added in the 1950s. The team opted to restore the façade, signage, diving board, and red marble walls and columns that it has long been known for. “While adapting historic buildings to meet modern needs, our goal is always to respect and reinterpret their original spirit,” says co-founder Aaron Clarke. 

This philosophy translates to the F&B spaces, too. Little Torch, the cocktail lounge that rekindles the atmosphere of 1970s nightlife through its design, juxtaposes glass brick walls with onyx marble tables and references to the profiles and geometries of Frank Lloyd Wright. 

The restaurant Pauline, named for the jet-setting Pauline Baker, wife of 20th-century cocktail writer Charles H. Baker, Jr., nods to her Caribbean travels through a motif that mimics the rippling sea and artwork magnifying mermaids and tropical settings. 

“We also wanted to pay homage to classic American diners, capturing their timeless essence,”explains ADC & Tuneu cofounder Marta Tuneu. So, there’s a wavy ceiling, 1950s-inspired banquette shapes, and rounded Art Deco windows that “create a subtle connection to the building’s broader architectural heritage.”

A respect for the city’s history and culture is a common thread in all these major renovation projects. Ennismore and Cain International’s vision for the property, realized in collaboration with Greece-based Elastic Architects, epitomizes this resurgence.

Schrager and Starck’s gleaming white, minimalist interventions in the 1990s contrasted greatly with architect Robert Swartburg’s 1947 classic Art Deco/Miami Modern version of the Delano. Today, its Art Deco façade, terrazzo flooring, hexagonal columns, buzzy pool, and Murano glass chandeliers have been fully restored. 

Like the rest of the Delano’s recent revitalization, Rose Bar’s intimate and conversational makeover also harkens back to the understated glamour and quiet luxury of mid-century Miami. This new space is a stark contrast to its days as a symbol for the hotel’s—and city’s—era of late 1990s/early 2000s excess. 

Unlike the exclusive but isolated concepts where celebs would hide out in Miami Beach’s rowdiest days “today’s guest experiences hospitality holistically,” he says. “That shift is real, and it is permanent.”

title: When in Beaune, Eat and Drink Like the Burgundian Winemakers Do
summary:
Just two hours by train from Paris, Beaune is the epicenter of Burgundy’s food and wine scene.

The post When in Beaune, Eat and Drink Like the Burgundian Winemakers Do appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Where to Eat
  • Caves Madeleine — A tasting menu built around local and seasonal ingredients paired with rare bottles.
  • Ma Cuisine — Traditional yet refined Burgundian cuisine with an ambitious by-the-glass list and deep cellar.
  • La Table du Square — Another fresh take on classic bistro fare with a relaxed dining room and easygoing service.
  • Soul Kitchen — Tiny 12-seater gastrobistro with a comforting menu driven by local suppliers.
  • Le Bacchus — Sleek dining room serving an exceptional burger topped with the region’s iconic Époisses cheese.
  • L’Expression — Elegant fine dining fit for a special occasion.
Where to Drink
  • La Maison du Colombier — Gatstropub well-suited to everything from a light aperitif to extensive bottle exploration.
  • La Dilettante — Natural-leaning wine selection and simple food served in a cozy atmosphere.
  • Crème Café Comptoir — Casual café with exceptional coffee and solid glass pours.

Terroir is wine’s central idea, and nowhere is it more tangible than in Burgundy. The region’s wine capital Beaune, just two hours by train from Paris, is where that idea becomes easiest to grasp.

Within its compact, rampart-ringed center, this medieval town is home to top négociant houses and their old cellars, wine shops with impressive collections, stylish bars, and the Hospices de Beaune, a landmark and former hospital whose vineyard holdings still anchor Burgundy’s most famous wine auction. Moving between them all—over polished cobblestones, along the canal, and past windows revealing candlelit rooms with antique furnishings—is an experience in itself. In any season, Beaune is effortlessly charming.

But the town has given wine lovers even more reasons to visit in recent years. Among the town’s most significant recent additions is Cité des Climats et vins de Bourgogne. Through maps, sensory displays, and tastings, the interactive center helps visitors decode Burgundy’s 1,247 climats and explains why a few meters of slope, soil, or exposure can change the identity of a wine. Think of it as a crash course before setting out along the Route des Grands Crus, which threads together the Côte d’Or’s most important wine villages.

Where wine lovers gather around great bottles, serious food is rarely far behind. Beaune is home to one of France’s most vibrant dining scenes. We asked local winemakers where they like to go for a glass or dinner—and which addresses still offer real value on the wine list.

Where to Eat in Beaune

All roads in Beaune lead to Caves Madeleine. “If I had to choose based on simplicity and the quality of the cooking, [this] would be at the top of my list,” says Clément Colin of Pierre-Yves Colin-Morey in Chassagne-Montrachet. 

Around a long candlelit oak table, corks are pulled on bottles from Domaine Leroy and Philippe Pacalet, alongside non-Burgundian icons like Château Rayas and Pierre Overnoy. Winemakers are regulars and often arrange working rendezvous that usually end several bottles later than planned. Jeremy Seysses of Domaine Dujac loves both the wine list and the food here, where rare cuvées are paired with a tasting menu by Martial Blanchon, built around local and seasonal ingredients. In addition to a stellar cellar and a superb kitchen, Caves Madeleine also welcomes guests in four elegantly appointed rooms in a 14th-century wine estate, just eight minutes away on foot from the restaurant.

Another of Beaune’s gastronomic landmarks is tucked away on one of the town’s most beautiful cobbled streets. Ma Cuisine was opened by Pierre and Fabienne Escoffier in 1996 and reopened this February following an extensive renovation. Today, whitewashed vaults, designer chairs, a long oak bar, and eclectic porcelain set the tone for a relaxed yet elevated evening. This stylish bistronomic restaurant serves a refined take on traditional Burgundian cooking, with the escargots de Bourgogne and roast pigeon particularly worth ordering. The by-the-glass selection is ambitious, featuring names such as Cécile Tremblay, Dureuil-Janthial, and Bastian Wolber, and the cellar remains one of the strongest in the region. Sought-after producers including Comtes Lafon and William Kelley appear on the list with remarkably restrained markups.

Just a ten-minute walk away—though almost everything is within walking distance in Beaune—is another fresh take on French cuisine: La Table du Square, beloved by Baptiste Guyot of Domaine Baptiste Guyot. “Romain and his team create seasonal dishes, whether classic recipes or more contemporary interpretations,” he says. “The wine list is particularly impressive and is guided by experienced sommeliers.” Hanna Shaps of Maison Shaps is equally enthusiastic about the service: “I recommend it for a relaxed dinner when you want to take your time. Don’t miss the 36-hour confit lamb shoulder.” 

Just around the corner is Soul Kitchen, a tiny gastrobistro where Matthieu Guennal single-handedly welcomes guests, cooks, and serves in a 12-seat dining room with wooden floors and exposed beams. A chalkboard lists the restaurant’s local suppliers. The menu is honest and comforting, with the occasional unexpected flourish. “Get the house tarte à l’Époisses, made with Burgundy’s iconic washed-rind cheese,” says Guyot. He also recommends the burger served with delightfully funky Époisses at Le Bacchus, where Anna-Sophie Adao runs the dining room with effortless professionalism while Olivier Baduel quietly works with seasonal ingredients in the kitchen.

For a special occasion, Seysses recommends L’Expression. “The shared main courses—roast chicken, whole fish, and others—are terrific, and the wine list is deep,” he says. “The fennel, orange, and seabass salad is particularly memorable.”

Where to Drink in Beaune

Whether you’re stopping for an apéritif or hunting for your next favorite Burgundy, La Maison du Colombier is worth a visit. Seysses tells visitors to grab a drink and some small plates at the gastropub, part of a hotel with the same name that occupies a historic dovecote tower. La Dilettante is another of his favorites. It’s a wine shop that feels like the living room of an obsessive collector: shelves mounted on exposed brick are packed with bottle trophies and there’s an atmosphere that encourages lingering. The kitchen is equally worth exploring, says Seysses: “The food is simple, the wine selection leans towards natural wines, though there are plenty of other options as well, and it’s always tasty.”

Another excellent stop for a glass of Burgundy from a small producer is Crème Café Comptoir. A long, welcoming counter, fresh flowers, mismatched porcelain, and a serious commitment to coffee make it one of the town’s most inviting cafés. “It’s a lovely place to stop for a specialty coffee—not necessarily for wine,” says Colin of Pierre-Yves Colin-Morey. “Sometimes the body needs a break from tasting.”

title: What Wine Culture Is Really Like on Yachts, According to the ‘Below Deck’ Crew
summary:

The post What Wine Culture Is Really Like on Yachts, According to the ‘Below Deck’ Crew appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
If the term “chief stew” means something to you, chances are you watch Bravo’s Below Deck—the upstairs/downstairs reality series that explores the wild realm of charter yachts. 

In this world, the chief steward or stewardess is the head of interior (separate from exterior, or deck crew) and responsible for all aspects of hospitality. In addition to overseeing housekeeping, organizing shore excursions and onboard entertainment, and coordinating with the chef for meal services, one of the key aspects of yacht life that falls under the chief stew’s purview is wine.

While wine appears in just about every episode of Below Deck and its spinoffs, it rarely plays a starring role, save the occasional rosé supply crisis or minor pairing fiasco. (In summary: neighboring vessels aren’t reliable sources for acquiring emergency bottles, and pairings aren’t easy to pull off if the chef is intent on preparing a buffet, not courses.) 

But wine undoubtedly propels the social culture on yachts as much as the engines propel the vessels themselves. From selection and storage to service and sourcing, several Below Deck crew and cast members spoke to us about the inner workings of the yacht world’s wine scene.

On-Board Wine Culture

No matter the size and budget of a given yacht charter, staff and guests both bring a wide range of wine knowledge and expectations with them on board. Since chief stews have to wear multiple hats, they inevitably learn about wine on the job as they go.

“There’s not a lot of formal wine courses or education within yachting,” says Oriana Schneps, who appeared in Below Deck Adventure and is now the founder and owner of The Yacht Edit. “As much as we can try to educate ourselves, it is such a robust world of its own, and that’s often one of the most feared elements of service for stewards and stewardesses,” she says, “because a lot of them don’t come with a background to really curate a wine program on board.” Learning on the job comes with the territory though, as does access to high-end bottles that clients might select for their journeys.

Like with all aspects of yacht life, guests can have extremely specific preferences, or they can just want to have a good time with whatever is available. “There are obviously some really huge wine enthusiasts who tell you exactly what they want,” says Daisy Kelliher, who has held the chief stewardess role on Below Deck Sailing Yacht and Below Deck Down Under, and who also co-hosts a podcast about the industry, Yacht Mess. “It’s kind of like, there are those who want to learn to kite surf and get really committed to it,” she says, “but most people are like, ‘yeah, I’ll just go swimming in the sea.’” A range of good quality but approachable wines works for most clientele. 

“We always have those staple wines that everyone loves as backup,” says Katie Glaser, who appeared in Below Deck for one season and who continues to work in the yachting industry, “like Veuve for Champagne, Cakebread or Caymus for reds, and Whispering Angel since rosé is huge.” 

Given the budget required for either owning or chartering a yacht, even for a few days, sometimes wine preference is expressed not so much as a matter of grape or region, but as a financial flex. “[Certain clients] don’t actually care about the taste of wine,” says Hannah Ferrier, chief stewardess for multiple seasons of Below Deck Mediterranean. “It’s about how much you spent on the bottles.”

Storing and Serving Wine at Sea

Private yacht owners may build wine storage into their vessels, with racks, cabinets, and coolers for bottles and glassware, but that’s often not the case with charter yachts. “Smaller boats really don’t have that kind of capacity,” says Glaser, “so when you go to the islands and you have back to back charters, you end up stashing it everywhere possible. I’ve had cases at the end of my bed before.”

Wherever possible, wine is provisioned regularly, rather than in one large acquisition, since a season’s worth of wine kept on board also isn’t very good for the wine. “You generally don’t want to keep wine on a boat for too long,” says Kelliher. “Besides the fact that they’re not great places for storage, there’s the movement and temperature fluctuation.”

Movement may also inform what kind of glassware is available on a charter yacht, regardless of what guests are drinking, or what storage space is available. Some mega yachts have the relative steadiness of cruise ships, but with sailing vessels or smaller yachts, “we’re breaking glasses left, right, and center,” says Kelliher, especially in cases where guests may insist upon dining on deck, even in especially windy conditions. 

Sometimes guest expectations can swing the other way where glassware is concerned, though, making the crew’s life easier. “I’ve had Caymus and whatever else put in plastic glasses and guests haven’t really cared,” says Glaser.

You Want It? You Got It

Provisioning wine for a yacht charter is typically done client by client based on what is expressed in the all-important preference sheets the crew receive preceding each charter. In places such as Florida, Italy, or the South of France, where many yachting itineraries begin, “not only will there be very good wine shops, but they’re probably going to have dedicated wine provisioners for yacht services,” says Kelliher.

Whatever the client wants, the client gets—no matter how big the ask, or how seemingly insurmountable the logistics. “You don’t get to say no,” says Glaser. “We’ve had wine flown in on private jets, helicopters, you name it,” she says. “If they want it, you figure out how to get it.”

In remote locations where wine can’t be airlifted in, the interior crew finds themselves on a mad dash whenever and wherever the yacht is in port. “We all have those stories where we’re running through a town asking anyone to source XYZ,” says Schneps, which may involve buying out the supply of miniscule local shops or even talking restaurants into selling their entire stock of a given bottle. Considering the budgets often involved in yachting, “we would just offer them so much money that they couldn’t really say no to it,” says Ferrier.

With yachting as with dining, though, sometimes what a guest wants is simply attention, and wine is something that savvy chief stews can use to their advantage in making the client happy. 

“Most people that claim to know about wine don’t actually know about it, but they like to appear to know about it in front of their friends,” says Ferrier. “I would always make a point to seek those guests out [privately] and offer advice about what particular note in a wine will bring out a particular fruit in the starter, or that kind of thing,” she says. This gives the guest ammunition at the dinner table, both on the yacht and in the future. “You just know this guy is gonna be at Craig’s in L.A. in two months’ time, going, ‘Oh I know that wine goes perfectly with apricots.’”

title: If You Can’t Bring Americans to the Winery, Bring the Tasting Room to Them
summary:
With airfare reaching record highs, some wineries are embracing the economic advantage of running tasting rooms closer to where their drinkers live.

The post If You Can’t Bring Americans to the Winery, Bring the Tasting Room to Them appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Key Points

  • With rising airfare costs making travel more expensive, wineries are opening off-site tasting rooms nearer to where consumers live.
  • Urban tasting rooms tap into local foot traffic and help build customer relationships without requiring expensive long-distance travel.
  • Satellite locations also educate guests, offer distinct urban experiences, and entice tourists to visit distant primary vineyards in the future.

Your Instagram feed might be filled with photos of people in Mykonos, Capri, and St. Tropez for vacation, but for the vast majority of Americans, flying anywhere this summer is a pricey undertaking.

According to a recent travel inflation report, airfare costs have increased by 26.7% over the past year, primarily due to the steep price increases in jet fuel earlier this spring. Those rising fares impact consumer appetite for international as well as domestic travel, the latter of which has real implications for the wine industry, which relies heavily on traffic to wineries and tasting rooms, especially during the summer.  

While some wineries have attempted to attract visitors by lowering tasting room costs (which the same report shows has had mixed success), others are embracing a different, albeit more dramatic, alternative: opening tasting rooms tens or even hundreds of miles away from the vineyard. 

“There is an opportunity by reaching the customer where they live. There aren’t dominant strategies that are pointing in a proven path, but they are emerging,” says Rob McMillan, EVP & Founder of the Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) Wine Division, in the company’s direct-to-consumer annual report.

Chris Brockaway, founder of Broc Cellars, says that the biggest benefit of running a tasting room in Berkeley, rather than in the bucolic California vineyards he sources from, is capitalizing on all of the foot traffic in the Bay Area. “If someone is visiting San Francisco, but not going to wine country, they can still visit us,” he says. 

Allison Owen, president and founder of Napa-based winery Turks Head, which, in 2024, opened its tasting room in West Chester, Pennsylvania, takes a similar view.

“We believe that there are a lot of people who are interested in exploring and learning about California wine, but might not have the time, money, and resources to travel across the country to experience it,” she says. “For those that are avid wine travelers, we have been able to bring the California wine experience home to them so they can enjoy it more often.”

A Win-Win for Wineries and Wine Country Tourism

Downtown Napa has over fifty tasting rooms. While visitors benefit from being able to hop from one to another on bike or foot, the market is extremely saturated. That means tasting rooms have to work harder to vie for tourists’ precious time.

“We are different by design,” Owen says. “We are the only California tasting room in West Chester, PA, and a true destination where people who live close walk to, and others have traveled from hours away by car to visit with us and experience what we have to offer.”

Conversely, some wineries, like Troon Vineyard & Farm in Oregon’s Applegate Valley, have found that adding a little distance between their tasting room and vineyard is a surprisingly effective way to drive tourism to major wine regions.

“We are able to introduce guests to things they didn’t even know they were missing, and act as a concierge for them when they decide they are ready to make the trip to southern Oregon,” says Meg Ordaz, director of consumer sales at Troon, which has a tasting room in downtown McMinnville in the Willamette Valley. “That works both directions, [when guests] are planning a trip to the Willamette Valley, [because] we can say, here’s where you should go besides us.”

Ordaz says that the Troon team has leaned into being different from most of their friends and neighbors in the Willamette Valley by showcasing varieties like Mourvédre, Carignan, and Vermentino that flourish in another AVA within the same state, four hours away.

Hosting Away from Home

When the vineyard is out of sight, the role of tasting room employees becomes especially critical. They are responsible for painting a vivid picture of the wine’s terroir from hundreds of miles away.

“Location, climate, and soil type are hard to understand while in an urban setting, so we do group trips up to the vineyard multiple times per year to stay or camp overnight,” says Brockaway, whose team sources Broc Cellars’ grapes from all over the state. 

He says that the trip gives tasting room staff important color about the wines, which they can then pass on to visitors. For example, everybody remembers that Brachetto is typically the first varietal to come in from Fox Hill every year, because the team goes up to pick it together. 

Ultimately, tasting rooms located away from vineyards serve as a test of more than just the tasting room staff’s education—it challenges the wine’s ability to compel drinkers to both travel even further, and perhaps more importantly, embrace where they are.

“Our locations are very distinct from each other; in the Applegate Valley, we are out on the farm, a solid 20 to 25 minutes away from town,” says Ordaz. “It is beautiful, peaceful, and romantic… At our location in McMinnville, we are in the middle of a downtown area that is vibrant and bustling. We have lodging and restaurant partners just down the block. We have street festivals and parades.”

title: Meeting the Parents? Woo Them with These Wines
summary:
Whether your SO's parents are serious wine nerds or entry-level drinkers, these pro-approved bottles will win them over.

The post Meeting the Parents? Woo Them with These Wines appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Successfully meeting your significant other’s (S.O.) parents for the first time is all about balance. You should be talkative but not obnoxious, inquisitive but not interrogatory, complimentary but not insincere. Striking the perfect balance is difficult in any scenario, but it’s especially tricky with the added pressure of really, really wanting to win them over.

Then, to top off the stress, you have to decide on a gift. Luckily, wine is always a good idea, but choosing a bottle invites a slew of new balancing acts. Matt Kettmann, a Wine Enthusiast writer at large who reviews wines from California (Central Coast and Southern California) and Languedoc-Roussillon, says that the wine you choose should “impress on an intellectual level, satisfy a wide array of palates, and not break the bank.” 

Of course, there is no one-size-fits-all bottle. The wine that meets these requirements varies based on the parents’ preferences, which is why we rounded up recommendations for entry-level, intermediate, and advanced wine drinkers. 

When the time comes for the long-awaited “meet the parents” dinner, don’t fumble at the bottle shop. Keep this list handy, and let the wine speak for you. With any luck, it will say good things.

Entry-Level

Maybe they’re just getting started on their wine journey. Maybe they enjoy wine but don’t drink it very often. Regardless of the reasoning, there are plenty of people who just don’t think too hard about the wines they drink. All that matters is whether they like it—which really is the most important thing.

When shopping for entry-level wine drinkers, the best thing to do is choose a bottle that is lowkey and easy to drink. You don’t want anything too complex or intimidating, and you shouldn’t go too crazy price-wise. 

According to Reggie Solomon, a Wine Enthusiast writer at large who reviews wines from France and Spain among other regions, Albariño is a great choice: “Albariño says, ‘let’s get to know each other, and have lunch under the sun.’” It’s light, crisp, and easygoing. A zippy Albariño plus a sunny lunch equals the ideal setting for meeting the parents.

If the occasion is better suited to a red wine, consider this domestic recommendation from Wine Enthusiast writer-at-large Michael Alberty, who reviews wines across the U.S. He suggests a Gamay Noir from Oregon because of its approachable, fruit-forward characteristics: “I have yet to meet anyone who doesn’t like a Gamay Noir from Oregon.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Forjas del Salnés 2024 Leirana Albariño Albariño (Rías Baixas)

Pastry dough, tangerine peel and chamomile aromas waft from the glass along with a touch of yogurt and meadow grass. Citrus and subtle hints of sea salt breaststroke across the midpalate which finishes in a pool of river stone and lemon peel. Pair with oysters, moules frites, and Croque Monsieur. Editors’ Choice. 93 Points — Reggie Solomon

$34 JJ Buckley

Rodrigo Mendez & Alberto Orte 2023 Muti Albariño Albariño (Rías Baixas)

Candied aromas of caramel apple and butterscotch open on the nose along with tropical notes of mango tea and pastry cream. More reserved on the palate than the nose, the wine reveals tangy acidity that leans into crushed stone and freshly-shaved lemon peel. Pair with turkey burgers and falafel. Editors’ Choice. 94 Points — R.S.

$44 The Cellar d’Or

Westmount 2023 Gamay Noir (Willamette Valley)

Yowza. The wine’s blackberry and bittersweet dark chocolate aromas flex as notes of earth and strawberry watch in admiration. This is a juicy treat, as electric fence-level acidity amplifies tart dark raspberry and cedar flavors. Pour with ham and butter sandwiches; pour with confidence. Best Buy. 91 Points — Michael Alberty

$20 Westmount Wine Company

Intermediate

There are many mid-level wine drinkers who enjoy most of the wines they try and are always happy to expand their horizons. On the other hand, some intermediate wine drinkers are confident in what they like and don’t care to explore new bottles. This is where things can get a little rocky, but fear not. 

In Alberty’s opinion, a Sauvignon Blanc from Washington will please parents who are familiar with wine but aren’t complete connoisseurs. “They tend to pack a grassy punch,” he says, and will leave a lasting impression. This is a great choice to express confidence without being overwhelming. 

John Sumners, a Wine Enthusiast writer at large and reviewer of wines from Portugal and Northeast Spain, says that a Rioja Gran Reserva is another great option, noting that the aging requirements of the classification means it should be ready to drink. Tempranillo, the primary grape of Rioja, is dense yet smooth with plenty of fruity spices. “Best of all,” he says, “it’s got that little nudge of Iberian exoticism while still being familiar and unintimidating, all at a fair price.”

On the other hand, there are plenty of delicious domestic options. Kettmann recommends a Rhône-style blend from California’s Central Coast. “They show that you know a bit about Old World tradition,” he says, “but are far more accessible, juicy, and ready to drink than Bordeaux blends.” Typically made with a blend of Grenache, Syrah, and Mourvedre, these wines feature plenty of ripeness and fruit, especially when grown in California. Plus, Kettmann notes, they tend to hover around the right price point to show that “you care about good flavor but aren’t a splurging showboat.” 

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Guardian 2024 Angel Sauvignon Blanc (Columbia Valley (WA))

This Guardian Angel doesn’t look over your shoulder, but it does take you to a Hawaiian beach. Pineapple and fresh-cut grass aromas lead to flavors like guava, grapefruit and a saline quality similar to nori. With acidity as lively as an aiha’a-style hula dance, this Sauvignon Blanc will put the pep into your step. Break out the tuna poke, stat. 92 Points — M.A.

$26 Wine Solutions

Terah Wine Co. 2024 Castro Valley Ranch Rhône-Style Red Blend (Central Coast)

Cranberry, strawberry, light stone and fennel pollen aromas make for a very intriguing and inviting nose on this blend of 65% Syrah and 35% Grenache from a vineyard near Gilroy. The palate is very textural, giving a stage for brisk cranberry flavors to evolve into warmer flashes of maraschino cherry. 93 Points — Matt Kettmann

$32 Terah Wine Co.

VOCHÉ 2015 GRAN RESERVA Tempranillo-Graciano-Garncha (Rioja)

Flowering herbs, red and black cherries, mixed berries are well integrated with oak spices, picking up a sanguine and savory element through the finish. The Voché Gran Reserva feels classic while also mouthwatering, elegant and layered, with firm while fine tannins that linger in the palate promising even more with aging. Editors’ Choice. 94 Points — Elaine Chukan Brown

Inquire with the importer

Advanced

If your sweetheart’s parents are full-on oenophiles, it’s time to pull out the big guns. Sumners says that you want “something legitimately special without looking like you’re trying to prove that you’re smarter or cooler than them.”

Solomon suggests a Sancerre Rouge. Although not produced at the same volume as its white counterparts, Sancerre Rouge exists and it’s downright delicious. Made exclusively from Pinot Noir, the light-bodied wines tend to take on classic notes of delicate red fruits and spice with a soft minerality influenced by the soils. Sancerre Rouge shows that you “value beauty in unexpected places and where most people don’t look for it,” says Solomon. 

If Pinot Noir sounds like a good idea but exploring uncharted territory doesn’t, go with Sumner’s pick: a Pinot Noir from Santa Barbara. “The region has the upstart, garagiste factor and is packed with producers wine nerds love, all while maintaining a sense of now-established familiarity,” he says.

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Maison de Madeleine 2023 Rouge Pinot Noir (Sancerre)

Ruby and slightly-garnet in color, the wine draws you in with elegant aromatics. Spiced black plum opens on the palate followed by blackberry compote, black olive and raspberry. Grippy tannins parade the longevity of this bottling. Decant and drink now, or enjoy from 2028 onwards. 92 Points — R.S.

$32 Continental Fine Wine & Spirits

Sandhi 2023 Rinconada Vineyard Pinot Noir (Sta. Rita Hills)

This is a rather wondrous bottling, starting with juicy aromas of cherry that are expertly masked by dewy sagebrush notes that arise with persistence and poise. The snappy palate ranges from raspberry and cranberry to rose petal and hibiscus, and then that slow-rising wave of green sage and peppercorn makes for both delicious and intriguing complexity. 98 Points — M.K.

$37 Wine.com

Sea Smoke 2023 Southing Pinot Noir (Sta. Rita Hills)

There are expert levels of integration going on throughout this bottling, starting with the subtle yet persistent aromas of raspberry, cranberry, potpourri and light sagebrush that continually draw in the nose. The palate’s firm texture elevates the cherry compote, citrus rind and strawberry cream flavors, with a lingering sense of violet painting the corners. This will be exciting to watch for years. Drink now-2040. Cellar Selection. 97 Points — M.K.

title: The Man Behind the Wine World’s Coolest Events Has Cracked the Dinner Party Code
summary:
From silly icebreakers to take-home treats, Jermaine Stone reveals his top tips for hosting a vibey evening.

The post The Man Behind the Wine World’s Coolest Events Has Cracked the Dinner Party Code appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
A good dinner party is more than the little details—it’s about how it makes guests feel. 

No one knows this better than Jermaine Stone, host of the Wine and Hip Hop podcast and Tasting Notes from the Streets event series. Stone had always dreamed of a career in rap music until a temporary packing job at Zachys Wine Auctions drew him into the world of wine. After racking up over a decade of experience in fine wine auctions and retail, he launched the wine marketing firm Cru Luv Selections and found a way to combine his two passions: wine and hip hop. He began hosting dinner parties and larger wine events that showcased his favorite wines alongside his favorite music.

We spoke with Stone about his hosting necessities for intimate, relaxed, and memorable dinner parties. The next time you’re thinking of hosting one, don’t panic over spilled wine or burnt lasagna. Focus on fostering the right vibe instead, and you’ll be just fine.

Put Your Guests at Ease Before the Party Even Starts

Curating a vibe actually starts long before the dinner party, when guests inevitably ask, “Can I bring anything?” Stone believes that the answer to this question should always be “nothing but yourself,” which makes guests feel comfortable before they even arrive. When they do, the room should feel physically welcoming and “as intimate as possible,” especially when it comes to lighting. Candles are your best friend, but any type of dim lighting will do.

“The playlist is key too,” Stone says. “You cannot really describe a vibe. You have to feel it.” When creating a playlist, he tends to start with a general concept and shuffle through songs to find those that “evoke the feeling [he’s] looking for.” Other times, Stone will choose a specific song to serve as inspiration for the rest of the playlist and evening.

If you want to take the transportive vibes even further, base the night around a theme and let your guests forget about the real world. It’s OK to get a little absurd with it—in fact, that’s encouraged. For one dinner party, Stone hosted a Pusha T-themed evening during which he exclusively poured white wine and blocks of parmesan littered the tables in place of—erm—other white rocks. Many crazy stories were shared. 

“People get very comfortable very quickly when you approach things like that,” he says.

Greet Every Guest with a Drink

As soon as guests arrive, Stone insists on greeting every single person who steps through the door. At its simplest, this can be an inviting smile and welcoming handshake, but there are other ways to set the right tone.

“I greet every single person […] with a glass of sparkling wine, usually Champagne,” Stone says. While Champagne is always a good opener, it’s not a requirement. A welcome drink in any form can do wonders for getting the night off to a good start. Whether it’s a batched cocktail or an extravagant mocktail, this extra act will make your guest feel comfortable and relaxed. 

Welcome drink or not, Stone believes that the thoughtfulness and care of greeting each person individually is most important here. “I talk to them [and] just try to build some sort of rapport,” he says. “The value is in the intimacy.”

Don’t Be Afraid of Icebreakers (or Silliness)

Once you’ve set the mood and party-goers have started to arrive, Stone emphasizes the importance of proactively helping guests feel at ease. 

“As the host, you need to make sure that every single person has a great experience,” Stone says, noting that many people can be shy and need a little extra encouragement. Conversation starters and games are a great place to start—they don’t have to be anything like the dreaded icebreakers of middle school. For example, Stone likes to ask his guests how they initially became interested in wine or which movie character they’re most like. “For the record,” he says, “I’m Fantastic Mr. Fox.”

Don’t be afraid to be a little extra silly, either. In the same way that a wacky theme can have transportive powers, being open and genuine encourages others to be the same. As long as you’re genuinely excited to host, your guests will be able to feel it. 

“People could be anywhere in the world but they chose to be there with [you] that night,” Stone says. “Make it count.”

Give Guests a Memento to Take Home

At the end of the night, once all the wine has been drunk and plates licked clean, one final step is required to end the party on a high note: sending your guests home with a memento.

“It’s always great to have something to bring people back to that night,” Stone says. The gift  can be as simple as the recipe for your entrée or as complex as a handmade gift, like a polaroid in a homemade frame. Stone likes to pass around QR codes that link to the party’s playlist, which he curates himself. Music is an essential part of the evening’s vibe, so sharing the playlist is an easy yet heartfelt way to help guests keep the good energy going.

And who knows, reminiscing on the wonderful evening just might inspire a guest to become a host themselves.

Queue a never-ending cycle of dinner parties. Dinner parties forever.

Meet the Region Making the World’s Premiere Rosé

Rosé can often get the reputation as being an easy, breezy, by-the-pool wine. But experts know there’s that rosé and then there’s Provence rosé.

Home to the world’s most iconic rosés, Provence is entirely dedicated to rosé wines of precision, excellence, and diversity. As the global specialist, Provence has spent centuries perfecting every step of the process, from the vine to the glass. Its exceptional terroirs, rosé-focused expertise, and signature style have set the benchmark for rosé wines around the world.

Monotonous Provence is not, both stylistically and geographically. The world’s leading rosé region stretches 120 miles from Marseille in the west to Nice in the east, and 75 miles from the Mediterranean into the foothills of the Alps. Across the region, a vivid mosaic of vineyards, terroirs, and soil types that bring to life Grenache, Cinsault, and Syrah.

“Grenache can bring fruit, Cinsault often contributes freshness and elegance, and Syrah can add structure and complexity,” says Cody Wexler, editorial manager of Wine Enthusiast’s Tasting Department.

All these elements come together to make a region of wines that can match any meal or mood. 

To help break down the versatility and finesse of Provence, Wexler and Tasting Department Special Projects Coordinator, Ella Bennett pour up three glasses from the 3 appellations of Provence (Côtes de Provence, Coteaux d’Aix-en-Provence, Coteaux Varois en Provence), all while making a tres Provençal galette.

Watch the full video here and read on for highlights and excerpts.

Have either of you made a galette before?

CODY WEXLER: Not successfully. 

ELLA BENNETT: That’s okay. Making it together is half the fun, and we have a great Provence rosé to share.

Provence rosé in hand, Cody and Ella unpack three wines, one of each PDO defining Vins de Provence. There’s the AOP Côtes de Provence,  the region’s largest and most emblematic appellation. Shaped by the influence of the sea, cooling winds, varied elevations, and a remarkable diversity of limestone-rich soils, it produces rosés renowned for their freshness, elegance, vibrant acidity, and signature mineral character.

Stretching from the Durance River to the Mediterranean sea, over landscapes painted by Cézanne, AOP Coteaux d’Aix-en-Provence makes wildly versatile rosés that can withstand time in the cellar. Long, sunny days, little rainfall, and fierce wines creates supple, fruity wines with body, texture, and structure.

AOP Coteaux Varois en Provence highlights high-altitude vineyards, with peaks reaching 1,000 meters into the Sainte-Baume massif. At those heights, cooler temperatures and shelter from the salty maritime winds brings to life elegant, somm-loved wines with wild, floral aromatics and a clean, vibrant acidity.

The terroir is really unique here. The vineyards sit among narrow valleys with limestone-rich clay soils. The soils and growing environment play a huge role in shaping the wine’s character and texture.

With this rich diversity of style and terroir, Provence rosé can pair with a globe of feasts and flavors.

EB: I think people associate rosé with summer because it’s refreshing, but it’s really a food-friendly wine first.

So we’ve all just collectively decided to limit ourselves?

CW: Even today we’ve tasted wines with very different personalities. Some are great as an aperitif, some work beautifully with food, and some shine on their own through their complexity and structure.

Watch Cody and Ella compete to make their own Provençal galettes and learn more about rosés from Provence.

title: The Best American Wines to Enjoy This Labor Day and Beyond
summary:
From experimental reds and whites to classic expressions of sparkling, America’s increasingly diverse wines rival the best in the world.

The post The Best American Wines to Enjoy This Labor Day and Beyond appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Once stereotyped as being solely about power, intensity, and ripeness, American wine has entered a new era of diversity and quality. In California, New York State, and beyond, U.S. producers are crafting bottles with precision, elegance, and stylistic range, and disproving the stale perception that American wine is one-size-fits-all.

“I’m excited to see ever more unusual varieties gaining the attention they deserve,” says Wine Enthusiast Writer-at-Large Tom Capo, who cites Picpoul Blanc in Texas, off-beat Italian varieties in Sonoma, and Napa Valley Scheurebe as reasons he’s optimistic about the future of American wine. “Yes, in Napa, Cabernet is king, and in the Russian River Valley, Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are the heavyweights. But growers everywhere are branching out.”

From experimental, new-wave reds and whites to classic expressions of sparkling, these increasingly diverse wines rival the best in the world. Here are some of our favorites.

White Wines

Signal Ridge 2023 Signal Ridge Vineyard Chardonnay (Mendocino Ridge)

We are at the top of the Mendocino Ridge Coast, the aromatics are heady, ethereal, with windswept, stone fruit, citrus zest, savory herbs, and the saltiness of the sea air on the nose. Vibrant, alpine, saline, dried herbs, Gaja apple skin, White nectarine, Meyer lemon on the palate. You can enjoy it now; it has lots of life. Expressive with expansive length. Cellar Selection. 97 Points — Tonya Pitts

$65 Signal Ridge

Ria’s Wines 2024 Viva Riesling (Seneca Lake)

From an exciting new husband-and-wife team, this lakeside Riesling offers delicate aromas of lemongrass, green tea and lime blossom that become more bombastic with time aerating in glass. In the mouth, it’s a lovely combo of racy lemon pith acidity and slippery textural weight. Still young, this could evolve quite beautifully and complexly over time. Editors’ Choice. 95 Points — Christina Pickard

$30 Wine Deals

Royer 2023 548 Chardonnay (Eola-Amity Hills)

This is a “break out” wine for Royer that commands attention. Its lemon peel and wet slate aromas are joined by a rich, sweet orchard fruit flavor similar to peach pie. The light and airy wine floats across the palate with grace and ease, with nervy acidity along for the ride. Flavors of white grapefruit, lemongrass tea and a pronounced mineral quality seem to last forever. Just pour a glass of the 548 with a plate of gougères to be revered as a demi-god in your lifetime. The Willamette Valley now has another great Chardonnay to add to its already lengthy list. Editors’ Choice. 97 Points — Michael Alberty

$115 Royer Vineyard

Red Wines

Passing Time 2023 Cabernet Sauvignon (Horse Heaven Hills)

A rich aromatic burst of sweet, ripe Rainier cherries is counterpointed by notes of orange peel, pipe tobacco and the worn leather of a favorite baseball glove. With balance that a Cirque du Soleil performer would envy, flavors like redcurrants, pie crust, black coffee and cedar match nicely with velvety tannins and juicy acidity. Those flavors have space between them, requiring you to pay attention to each one thoughtfully. It is like a jazz musician trying to create a sense of anticipation. Pair with a nice steak and the oldest Miles Davis record you can find. Drink now through 2040. Cellar Selection. 97 Points — M.A.

$110 Passing Time

Wentworth 2024 Wentworth Vineyard Pinot Noir (Mendocino Ridge)

Lofty notes of deep dark berries cascade across the nose with dried floral, molasses, fresh herbs, and toasted French oak serenades into flavors on the palate of ripe red plum, youthful blackberries, raspberries, pomegranate, star anise, crushed bay leaf and juicy acidity on the finish. Aerate or cellar until 2038. Cellar Selection. 99 Points — Tonya Pitts

$135 Wentworth Vineyards

Ulysses 2021 Ulysses Cabernet Sauvignon (Oakville)

An excellent vintage meets an impressive site and deft winemaking for this exquisite Cabernet Sauvignon from the Ulysses project of Christian Moueix. Consistently a stand out cuvee, the 2021 delivers an alluring balance of pleasure, restraint, refinement, and seductive texture. Fresh violets and bay laurel lift a complex of spiced, dark fruits and espresso carrying into a lengthy mineral finish of graphite, gunmetal, and cocoa powder tannins. Balancing acidity brings harmony to a wine of innate intensity and concentration. This is a red wine to age as much as enjoy. A stand out. Cellar Selection. 98 Points — Elaine Chukan Brown

Inquire with the distributor

Build Your Dream Cellar

Rosé Wines

Tessier Winery 2024 Soul Love Red Blend (California)

This low-intervention wine is dry, primarily Riesling, blended with Gamay Noir, Mourvèdre, and much love. It is another in a series of offerings in honor of musicians—this one is an ode to David Bowie’s Ziggy Stardust era. The aromas are strawberry, cherry, melon, white flower, and mineral on the nose. The palate is tangerine and raspberry, with a dash of coriander. It is crushable and delicious with a bit of chill. Grab it before it’s gone! 93 Points — T.P.

$29 Wine Chateau

Lu & Oly 2024 Flowerhead Rosé (Columbia Valley WA)

The scent of a raspberry daqcuiri with a salted rim is an absolute invitation to dive into this wine with reckless abandon. In the background, a puff of talc makes itself known. There is plenty of acidity here to accompany a tart raspberry lemonade flavor that threatens any thirst to avoid being quenched. This is one heck of a nice pink wine. Best Buy. 92 Points — Michael Alberty

$28 My Wine Connection

South Shore Wine Co. 2024 The Perfect Rosé Rosé (Lake Erie)

South Shore Wine Co. offers spriteliness in its 2024 ‘Perfect Rose.’ The nose evokes stone fruit, rose petal and a wet rock minerality. The palate is electric. Peach and nectarine dominate while rose petal offers a lift on the mid-palate. The finish is long. Drink now. Best Buy. 92 Points

$16 Mazza

Sparkling Wines

Schramsberg Vineyards 2016 J. Schram Rosé Sparkling Blend (North Coast)

This one is hugely red berries, cream, and fresh on the nose: the bubbles are racing towards the surface of the glass—it is like you stuck your nose in a bowl of fresh, ripe, ready-to-eat berries. It rounds out creamy, firm brioche mousse, slices of strawberry, mandarin orange, red plum, blood orange meat, smashed clove, and well-integrated minerals and acidity. 98 Points — T.P.

$148 Wine Chateau

Roederer Estate 2007 L’Ermitage Brut Late Disgorged Sparkling Blend (Anderson Valley)

Soft, tiny bubbles rising toward the glass’s surface, with aromas of baked golden apple, roasted pears, peach, orange blossoms, and cinnamon. The mid-palate is firm mousse, on the palate, pineapple, white nectarine, sugared White grapefruit, papaya, brown sugar vanilla cream with a long dry sumptuous finish. Editors’ Choice. 98 Points — T.P.

$120 Roederer Estat

Red Tail Ridge Winery NV Réserve Perpétuelle Change, Cuvée Nº 5 Chardonnay-Riesling (Finger Lakes)

This is an excellent sparkler, by all accounts; all toasty, yeasty goodness on the nose, the subtle citrus, stone fruit and floral characters tucked just beneath. There’s satisfyingly vigorous, long-lasting fizz, a touch of residual sugar that’s countered by mouthwatering acidity, and delicate white blossom and fruit tart flavors that linger on the finish. A classy drop that deftly demonstrates New York’s sparkling prowess. Editors’ Choice. 94 Points — Christina Pickard

$27 Empire Wine

title: Not Sure What to Pair with Breezy Warm-Weather Meals? Try Light Reds
summary:
Industry pros share their favorite light reds to match with classic summer dishes, from grilled chicken to black bean burgers.

The post Not Sure What to Pair with Breezy Warm-Weather Meals? Try Light Reds appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
As the dog days of summer continue, warmer weather calls for lighter, leaner wines that are fruit-forward and fresh. Sure, rosé and crisp whites are predictable pairings for summer salads and seafood, but don’t think you have to rule out red wine until fall. 

Lower in tannins and alcohol (typically falling around 13% or less), lighter reds are versatile enough to pair with delicate shrimp ceviche and plank-seared salmon to richer, more sophisticated plates like grilled chicken paillard.

Look to varieties like Pinot Noir, Gamay, and Grenache—plus less-expected Sicilian Frappato and Austrian Blaufränkisch—for the right recipe of acidity, vibrancy, and fruit to complement even the toughest-to-pair plates. With younger, lighter-bodied reds, give them a little chill to brighten up the red fruit notes and lessen the tannins while still keeping the integrity of the wine intact.

We polled industry pros on their favorite light reds to match summer’s best dishes. All you have to do is fire up the grill and start pouring.

Cedar Plank Grilled Salmon with California Pinot Noir

Pinot Noir is a go-to pairing for this grilled salmon recipe, as it cuts the richness of the fish while enhancing the subtle smokiness from the cedar plank and herbal notes of the spice rub. Jacob Brown, head sommelier at Realm Cellars in Napa Valley, thinks a Pinot Noir from the Russian River Valley makes an excellent match.

“Grilling culture and California wines evolved together, and pairing fish with red wine is part of that shared story,” he says. “Don’t shy away from this combination—the rustic, primal character of grilled salmon, especially with a bit of char from the cedar, is beautifully complemented by the bright red fruit and savory nuance of a Pinot Noir. It’s a pairing that feels both grounded and elevated.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Harper’s Rest 2023 Moon Dust Vineyard Pinot Noir (Russian River Valley)

Gorgeous aromas of tart cherry, spiced plum compote, roses, and black tea drive the nose of this Pinot. The palate brings in rounded tannins, fresh acidity, and flavors of pomegranate, cedar, flowers, herb mélange, and dusty cocoa across a long and winding finish. Editors’ Choice. 95 Points — Tom R. Capo

$72 Flatiron Wines

New England Clambake with Gamay 

While beer might come to mind as the natural pairing for a clam bake, consider the light red instead. “Gamay is a great partner for a New England clambake,” says Kevin Goyenechea, general manager and sommelier at Huso in New York. “Its bright red fruit, vibrant acidity, and low tannins make it refreshingly compatible with shellfish, sweet corn, and smoky sausage—all without overwhelming the dish’s fresh flavors.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Samuel Louis Smith 2024 Baytree Lane Vineayrd Gamay Noir (Sonoma Valley)

This young Central Coast superstar headed north for Gamay this vintage, and the results fall in line with his lithe style. Quite transparent in the glass, the wine pops on the nose with wet stone and white pepper aromas that decorate the racy core of strawberry water and raspberry granita. The palate is vibrant, spicy, refreshing and, ultimately, a whole lot of fun. 94 Points — Matt Kettmann

$33 K&L Wine Merchants

White Fish in Beurre Blanc with Frappato

The classic French butter sauce (beurre blanc) from the Loire Valley requires only a few ingredients—unsalted butter, shallots, white wine, vinegar, and cream—but provides a world of flavor when drizzled over fish. A dry Chenin Blanc is a great pairing, but Frappato, a fruit-forward Sicilian red varietal, is a low-tannin, high-acidity alternative that can cut through the sauce’s buttery richness.

“The red berry and floral notes add a lively, elegant contrast without overpowering the delicate fish,” explains Goyenechea.

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Arianna Occhipinti 2023 Il Frappato Frappato (Terre Siciliane)

On the nose, violets, wild cherries and wild strawberries pop above a backbone of pepper and crushed herbs. The palate has an incredible freshness, but also profundity. Frappato always feels especially connected to the earth, tethered to something deep underneath us. Arianna has a special talent for teasing out that sensation. 95 Points — Danielle Callegari

$40 Envoyer Fine Wines

Roasted Halibut with Etna Rosso

“I love the challenge of pairing fish with a light red—it’s a great way to surprise your guests with what many consider a nontraditional pairing,” says Nicole Castro, wine director of New Jersey sister restaurants Lita and Judy & Harry’s, who often looks to island wines from Sicily, Mallorca, or the Canaries. 

Since this halibut recipe calls for Sicilian Castelvetrano olives and capers, Castro suggests matching the dish with a mineral-driven Etna Rosso, crafted from Sicily’s native Nerello Mascalese. “Wines from the volcanic soils of Mount Etna are often high-toned and fresh, with an herbaceous backbone,” she adds.

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Benanti 2023 Contrada Monte Serra Nerello Mascalese (Etna)

Incredibly vibrant and dynamic—the volcanic energy of Etna rumbling under the intensity of the Sicilian sun that gives rise to an immense fertility. Stimulating. 96 Points — D.C.

$59 Saratoga Wine

Shrimp Ceviche with Chilean País

For a dish with as much acidity and herbaceousness as shrimp ceviche, Castro recommends reaching for a light, juicy Chilean País—and giving it a chill. “Chile is a seriously underrated wine region, which means you can find some incredible value wines,” she says. “País is also known as the Mission grape or Listán Prieto in other parts of the world, and in the right hands, it gets really bright, funky, and fresh.”

A French Poulsard would also work well here, since the notes of wild strawberry, cranberry, and red currant echo the tangy citrus and tomato in the dish, while offering a soft sweetness that balances the heat and acidity, explains Basile Al Mileik, partner and wine director at Fedora in New York. “It’s one of the lightest red grape varieties in the world, with a translucent body that won’t overwhelm the marinated shrimp,” he adds. “Subtle earthy undertones ground the high-toned brightness of the ceviche, adding a touch of complexity without stealing the show.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Gillmore 2023 Mariposa País (Maule Valley)

A bouquet of fresh roses and berries introduces a simple palate. Subtle strawberry flavors are backed by moderate acidity and gentle tannins. This light-bodied and chillable red will pair well with pizza. Best Buy. 88 Points — Jesica Vargas

$15 K&L Wine Merchants

Black Bean Burger with Spätburgunder 

The crunch from the panko breadcrumbs and smoky, slightly sweet hint from the chipotle peppers in these black bean burgers pair perfectly with the freshness of Spätburgunder, a.k.a. German Pinot Noir. “Think of cherries, olives, flowers, and a touch of earthy minerality,” says Austrian-born sommelier Katja Scharnagl (formerly of Le Bernardin in New York), who suggests looking at wines from the Baden area, near the borders of France and Switzerland.

Another light, herbaceous option is a cool-climate Cabernet Franc. “With cumin and chipotle in the mix, it’s a great opportunity for a ‘like with like’ pairing,” adds Castro. “Loire or Finger Lakes Cab Francs often show a jalapeño or peppercorn note that plays right into the burger’s smoky, spiced profile.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Heitlinger 2020 Pinot Noir (Baden)

A super juicy and expressive Pinot Noir that offers a generous mix of ripe plum, baking spice, and delicate cocoa notes. The wine is beautifully balanced, with a fresh acidity that provides great energy and lift, ensuring it stays vibrant throughout. 90 Points — Aleks Zecevic

$30 Yiannis Wine

Roasted Chicken with Grenache

With its smooth texture, bright red fruit flavors, and subtle earthy notes, Grenache is the perfect pairing for a one-pan dish like roasted chicken, according to Goyenechea. “The wine’s gentle tannins and refreshing acidity complement the tender meat and crispy skin, while its peppery spice enhances the seasoning in the dish,” he says. “Whether with rosemary, garlic, or paprika, Grenache’s versatility makes it a perfect match.”

Alternatively, Scharnagl suggests a Blaufränkisch from Burgenland in Austria. “Blaufränkisch is best described as a Pinot Noir and a Syrah who met and decided to move in with each other,” she jokes. “It has spice, some red fruit, elegance, finesse, and just enough body that it pairs great with a lot of dishes—especially roasted chicken!” 

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Echolands 2024 Grenache (Walla Walla Valley (WA))

I love this light and airy take on Grenache. From its 13.4% ABV to its vigorous acidity, this is grace personified. First, there are the wine’s aromas of marionberries, cranberry ice, orange and just a hint of thyme. Then you get juicy lingonberry, sage and black coffee flavors that feel like they are floating along a lithe and nimble mouthfeel. Give me a hammock, a sunset and a glass of this wine and I will be a happy camper. Editors’ Choice. 94 Points — Michael Alberty

$40 Echolands Winery

Grilled Chicken Paillard with Nebbiolo 

In its younger, fresher form, Nebbiolo, the same grape behind Piedmont’s big Barolos, shines alongside a dish like this grilled chicken paillard, pairing beautifully with the sweet smokiness of the peaches, richness of the gouda, and salinity from the Sicilian olives. 

“When young and not aged in oak, a Langhe Nebbiolo jumps with bright red fruit and acidity while still having layers of complexity to intertwine with all the different components in this dish,” says Tommy Voter, director of operations for Italian restaurants Bar Mutz, Viaggio, and Osteria Crescendo in New Jersey. “Those tannins we all love are dialed back with a slight chill that doesn’t overpower the freshness of a chilled summer red.

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

San Lorenzo Alto 2022 Nebbiolo (Langhe)

Fresh cherries mingle with rose buds while crushed stones and mountain herbs soar from these dramatic 600-meter heights. The palate unfolds like Hemingway’s prose, where years of mentorship and regional immersion reveal themselves through waves of complexity. Each sip tells new tales, where pristine fruit and noble tannins unlock layers upon layers, sometimes necessitating a pause to collect oneself. For a debut release, this wine speaks with the wisdom of an old soul, proving that some first chapters read like instant classics. 2026-2050. Cellar Selection. 95 Points — Jeff Porter

$34 Leon & Son

Tofu Salad with Gamay

Tofu is nearly neutral in taste and typically relies on a sauce or marinade for flavor. To match the umami-packed, nori-marinated tomatoes that star in this tofu salad recipe, Alex Anderson, beverage director at Peychaud’s in New Orleans, suggests a chilled, peppery Gamay. 

“This tofu salad has a lot of bold Japanese notes,” she explains. “The lightness of the wine will not overwhelm the dish, and the raspberry and white pepper notes will pair well with the brightness of the fresh tomatoes and ginger.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Domaine André Colonge et fils 2024 Gamay Noir (Fleurie)

This wine is dripping with finesse. Intoxicating aromas of red raspberry, muddled strawberry and boysenberry open on the nose buttressed by pomegranate and dried violet blossom. Pillowy tannins recede into plush, mature red fruit that flirts with chalk on the finish. You can drink now, but this wine will continue to develop in bottle through 2031. Editors’ Choice. 94 Points — Reggie Solomon

title: The Latest Miami Design Trend Signals a Departure from Debauchery
summary:
While mega-clubs continue to rage, Miami’s once hedonistic hotel scene is shapeshifting into something more subdued.

The post The Latest Miami Design Trend Signals a Departure from Debauchery appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
At its heyday in the 1990s, the Rose Bar, the lobby lair at Delano Miami Beach, exemplified the city’s once-ravenous predilection for the debauched and the flashy. 

The illuminated quartz bar was always packed with Cosmo-sipping women in Manolos and the Hollywood set, including supermodels, actors, and A-List musicians like Lenny Kravitz, who designed the hotel’s nightclub, the Florida Room. Madonna was part-owner of the hotel’s Blue Door restaurant and celebrated her 37th birthday on the property.

In 1995, when visionary hotelier Ian Schrager and French designer Philippe Starck transformed the tired Art Deco beauty into an upscale destination resort, they simultaneously ignited a new chapter of anything-goes, wee-hours revelry.

“There were the cool rock star people, there were the Hollywood billionaire types, the downtown fashion New York people, people swimming naked in the pool at 1 am,” trainer David Barton, whose gym had a branch in the hotel for several years, told the New York Times. “You were just in this other world.”

That world may be dead—or, at least changing. 

After a multi-year, multimillion-dollar revamp, Delano Miami Beach has just reopened its doors with a classier, calmer vibe that’s more focused on wellness and fine dining than indulgence. Rose Bar may be back, but its surrealistic design with pink walls and lighting has given way to a cozier deep red, moody palette that is more about intimacy and connection than showing off.

There’s also a spa starring a 22-seat sauna and a private members’ retreat that signal a departure from clubby vibes and celebrity gawking to a less debaucherous form of socializing that resonates with today’s well-heeled travelers.

It’s not just the Delano that’s delicately balancing nostalgia with a fresh, contemporary aura. Art Deco and Miami Modern legends around town are in the midst of a rebrand.

A New Era of Miami Nightlife

Despite the mega-clubs that continue to rage, Miami’s hedonistic days are shapeshifting into something more subdued. As some of the city’s landmark hotels find new life, rowdiness is in the rearview mirror.

The 1940s Collins Avenue fixture, The Raleigh Hotel, which was spruced up by infamous hotelier André Balazs in 2004, is currently being developed by Rosewood Hotels & Resorts. Next year, the Auberge Collection is slated to unveil its reboot of the 1949, Albert Anis-designed Shore Club.

This latest turning point for the city and its tourism scene is proving that Miami’s Art Deco institutions are increasingly moving away from one-dimensional glamour and embracing the easygoing desires of contemporary travelers.

“What we are seeing globally, and Miami reflects this acutely, is a fundamental shift in what sophisticated travelers value. The era of purely scene-driven hospitality has given way to experiences that build intentionally, where dining, music, design, and atmosphere function as a single cohesive narrative rather than separate offerings,” explains Rizwan Kassim, CEO of Paris Society, the French hospitality company behind Rose Bar’s revitalization and the other food and beverage outlets in the Delano Miami Beach. 

For Gigi Rigolatto, a bright, boisterous restaurant buoyed by access to the Delano’s pool, Paris-based architect and designer Hugo Toro melded carved wood, yellow Siena marble, and coral stone. At the property’s Mimi Kakushi, the Dubai import that only guests and members can access, diners are transported to 1920s Osaka with wooden screens, hand-painted walls, and cinematic lighting courtesy of London studio Pirajean Lees. Conjuring these two disparate worlds was deliberate, Kassim points out, because “Miami has evolved significantly, and the hospitality landscape has had to evolve with it.”

In other Art Deco hotels, that evolution means honoring the natural scenery and culture. When overhauling the soon-to-open Royal Palm South Beach Miami, part of Marriott’s Tribute Portfolio collection, Malcolm Berg, president and design director of Coral Gables-based architecture and design firm EoA Group, opted for a restrained coastal sensibility mixing stone, wood, and plaster with stripes and sun-washed tones as opposed to the too-trendy, dated interiors defining the hotel’s most recent chapter. 

The new Royal Palm is “less about spectacle as identity and more about experience as daily life,” he says. To create what he calls “a continuous social landscape,” each individual space flows into one another including the fluid ensemble of F&B spaces that celebrate Miami’s motley neighborhoods. Cuban coffee and pastries call to mind Little Havana at Compass Rose, which uses the hotel’s vintage green-glass reception desk repurposed as a counter that evokes the Art Deco period. The poolside bar Paloma Club’s vivid yellow and blues speak to artsy neighborhoods like Wynwood. And the lush ambiance at rum bar, Mixed Company, encapsulates the exuberance of South Beach itself.

“The idea is that guests are almost on their own culinary tour through Miami as they move through the hotel, but it never feels forced,” says Garron Gore, senior director of restaurant & bar development at Davidson Restaurant Group. “There are still those fun, over-the-top moments Miami is known for, whether that is a tableside cocktail experience with glassware chilled to negative 40 degrees or fresh ceviche prepared tableside at the pool, but the overall atmosphere is more relaxed and approachable.”

Weaving in the ‘Tropical Deco’ Past

While these hotel redesigns are adapting to today’s laid-back travelers, they’re not necessarily shedding the Art Deco and Miami Modern accents that date back to the 1930s and ‘40s. The period, often dubbed “Tropical Deco,” provided a sleek, uplifting counterpoint to the long, gloomy Great Depression that had finally just faded away. The design teams responsible for the makeovers of these properties are carefully contemplating which elements to preserve.

For the Shelborne by Proper, the newest incarnation of the circa-1941 Collins Avenue property, Barcelona design studio ADC & Tuneu studied the original colors and lines of the Miami Modern property, such as the original ribbon windows and open-air breezeways, and the floating staircase that was added in the 1950s. The team opted to restore the façade, signage, diving board, and red marble walls and columns that it has long been known for. “While adapting historic buildings to meet modern needs, our goal is always to respect and reinterpret their original spirit,” says co-founder Aaron Clarke. 

This philosophy translates to the F&B spaces, too. Little Torch, the cocktail lounge that rekindles the atmosphere of 1970s nightlife through its design, juxtaposes glass brick walls with onyx marble tables and references to the profiles and geometries of Frank Lloyd Wright. 

The restaurant Pauline, named for the jet-setting Pauline Baker, wife of 20th-century cocktail writer Charles H. Baker, Jr., nods to her Caribbean travels through a motif that mimics the rippling sea and artwork magnifying mermaids and tropical settings. 

“We also wanted to pay homage to classic American diners, capturing their timeless essence,”explains ADC & Tuneu cofounder Marta Tuneu. So, there’s a wavy ceiling, 1950s-inspired banquette shapes, and rounded Art Deco windows that “create a subtle connection to the building’s broader architectural heritage.”

A respect for the city’s history and culture is a common thread in all these major renovation projects. Ennismore and Cain International’s vision for the property, realized in collaboration with Greece-based Elastic Architects, epitomizes this resurgence.

Schrager and Starck’s gleaming white, minimalist interventions in the 1990s contrasted greatly with architect Robert Swartburg’s 1947 classic Art Deco/Miami Modern version of the Delano. Today, its Art Deco façade, terrazzo flooring, hexagonal columns, buzzy pool, and Murano glass chandeliers have been fully restored. 

Like the rest of the Delano’s recent revitalization, Rose Bar’s intimate and conversational makeover also harkens back to the understated glamour and quiet luxury of mid-century Miami. This new space is a stark contrast to its days as a symbol for the hotel’s—and city’s—era of late 1990s/early 2000s excess. 

Unlike the exclusive but isolated concepts where celebs would hide out in Miami Beach’s rowdiest days “today’s guest experiences hospitality holistically,” he says. “That shift is real, and it is permanent.”
